source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Across the literature, chain of thought (CoT) pays off almost only on math, symbolic and logic tasks. On other tasks it gives about nothing.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 110 papers, 1,218 CoT-vs-direct comparisons. Mean gain: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logic 6.9 points. Those three categories: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. All other categories: 56.8 vs 56.1. Own runs on many models and datasets agree (gains up to 41.6 points on MATH, 66.9 on GSM8K).
limits: Not code-specific. Averages hide the weak-model case. Gains measured with zero-shot/few-shot CoT, not scaffolds.
agent_relevance: Tracing code is a symbolic task, so S2 sits in the zone where written steps help. Use the pilot gate (G11) only to find the weak-model exceptions, not to doubt CoT in general. Gap 3.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (planning vs execution split)
finding: Authors split symbolic tasks into planning (write a formal plan) and execution (run the plan). CoT helps mostly on the execution step. An external tool beats CoT at execution.
numbers: GSM8K and logic sets (ContextHub, FOLIO). Plan+Direct solver gives little over direct answer; Plan+CoT solver and CoT give most of the gain; Plan+Tool solver (Python interpreter or Z3) beats both in most models and datasets.
quote: CoT primarily helps with the execution step that performs computation and symbolic manipulation, but falls short of what LLMs with tool augmentation can do.
limits: Tool arm used a model-written plan; unparseable plans were counted wrong (guess if multiple choice). Ceiling effects on strong models.
agent_relevance: Direct support for code-run over in-head trace when the step is pure execution (gap 9). A written trace beats a bare guess but loses to real execution.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: When the cost of repair is counted (tokens, not just pass rate), self-repair gives modest, uneven, sometimes zero gain. The bottleneck is the model's feedback on its own code.
numbers: Code Llama 13B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS. On APPS only GPT-4 gains clearly from self-repair; Code Llama and GPT-3.5 mostly match or lag the plain resampling baseline at equal budget. At small budgets gains are marginal or absent.
limits: Feedback here is model-written text about the failing code plus test results, not a real execution trace. Models from 2023.
agent_relevance: Strong support for comparing at equal tokens (G11). A weak model should resample rather than revise on its own feedback. Gaps 2, 3, 9.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (human feedback study)
finding: Better feedback text lifts repair a lot. A stronger model's feedback helps weak models. Expert human feedback beats GPT-4's own feedback for GPT-4 repair.
numbers: 16 participants, 2 feedback texts for each of 40 failing GPT-4 programs. Repair success with GPT-4 feedback 33.30% overall (intro 42.64, interview 19.33, competition 3.67); with human feedback 52.60% (62.21, 45.67, 14.67). Code Llama and GPT-3.5 beat both baselines on APPS when given GPT-4 or GPT-3.5 feedback.
limits: Human feedback is natural-language diagnosis, not execution data. Small N of programs (40). Human effort not priced.
agent_relevance: What matters is the quality of the diagnosis in the revision slot. A real trace helps only if it makes the diagnosis better. Gap 2.

source: Wu et al. (2026) DebugRepair: Enhancing LLM-Based Automated Program Repair via Self-Directed Debugging
finding: Giving the repair model real runtime values (print-instrumented traces from running the failing test) beats giving it only the failure symptoms (stack trace, error). The ablation removes the trace and loses about a quarter of fixes.
numbers: Defects4J, GPT-3.5 backbone, full method 224 correct fixes. Without simulated debugging (symptoms only): 165 correct (-26.3%); 213 plausible (-24.7%). Without test purification: 164 (-26.8%); purification cuts runtime-output tokens by 18.6%. Average 38,000 tokens per bug, vs 210,000 (ChatRepair) and 270,000 (RepairAgent). DeepSeek-V3: 295 correct fixes. Five other backbones averaged +51.3% over vanilla.
quote: Without runtime traces, the framework has to rely only on static, outcome-level error information
limits: Java bugs, not Python edge cases. Ablation run on GPT-3.5 only (weak model). The paper notes that for simple single-line bugs the extra trace text can make context longer and slightly harder. Authors' own system, v1 preprint, not independently replicated. Tokens compared across different papers' budgets, not equal-token controlled.
agent_relevance: Best direct answer to gap 2 so far: trace beats error-message only, and trace text must be cut down (slice to the failing path). But not shown for frontier models at equal tokens.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Telling a model to review and fix its own answer, with no outside signal, does not help and often hurts. The same loop helps only when an oracle tells it the answer was wrong. Showing the truth next to the guess is an outside signal.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CSQA 89.7, HotpotQA 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, CSQA 85.5, HotpotQA 59.0. For GSM8K GPT-3.5 retained the first answer 74.7% of the time and changed correct to wrong more often than wrong to correct.
limits: Math and QA, not code. Oracle labels leak the answer, so oracle gains are an upper bound, not a fair test. Table layout in the text extraction was garbled; the numbers were matched to rows with care.
agent_relevance: The conflict operator (O3) should be fed by real execution output, never by the model's own judgement that its trace looks wrong. Gap 5 partly closed: external signal helps, self-judgement does not.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Correcting a model-written program with the real interpreter's output works. Removing the interpreter (the same loop with the model critiquing itself) gives a small gain or a loss.
numbers: Text-davinci-003 on GSM8K: CRITIC with tool +2.1 over program-of-thought; CRITIC without tool -1.8 (stated in text). On TabMWP both help (+23.0 with tool, +20.3 without in the table, much of it format repair). Gains grow with model size (TabMWP +4.7, +9.4, +16.0 for 7B, 13B, 70B).
quote: Without execution feedback from the interpreter, the ability of LLMs to correct programs becomes limited and unstable.
limits: 2023 models, math/table programs not trace-reading. Table cells reconstructed from garbled extraction; trust the prose figures. Not equal-token.
agent_relevance: Supports feeding actual run output into revision and not trusting the model's own review. Gaps 2, 5.

source: Markosyan et al. (2025) What I Cannot Execute, I Do Not Understand: Training and Evaluating LLMs on Program Execution Traces (trace formats)
finding: Trace format matters, but only measured after fine-tuning. A compact trace that writes only the variables that changed per line beat the full state dump on loops. On short CRUXEval programs the two were about equal.
numbers: Fine-tuned models. CRUXEval output: direct-output tuning 49.3%; full scratchpad 78.7%; compact (diff) scratchpad 79.7%; line-1 73.3%; line-n 60.8%. MBPP functions with nested loops (avg 58 to 74 executed lines): direct 47.3%; full scratchpad 64.5%; compact 77.4%; compact + step-in 80.6%. Process accuracy 76.3% compact vs 64.5% full.
limits: All numbers are for tuned models, not prompted frontier models. No free-form arm. Gains from diff format come on long traces; on short ones nothing.
agent_relevance: Closest data to gap 4: structured line-state format is the unit tested; diff format (changed vars only) saves tokens and helps on loops. No test yet of structured vs free-form on prompted untuned models; gap 4 stays open.

source: Markosyan et al. (2025) What I Cannot Execute, I Do Not Understand: Training and Evaluating LLMs on Program Execution Traces (prompted vs tuned, cost of long traces)
finding: Authors show error modes under tracing: string indexing and tokenization of literals; one wrong step out of 20 breaks the answer. Dynamic scratchpads (state rewritten, not accumulated) win on very long runs.
numbers: Long executions up to 14k steps handled by dynamic scratchpad; compact and full scratchpads beat dynamic ones on CRUXEval because those runs are short. Step-error compounding: process accuracy 74-77% per trace on MBPP loops.
limits: Fine-tuned small models. Token cost per trace depends on executed lines (avg 73.9 lines for loops).
agent_relevance: Token cost of a full trace grows with executed lines, so long loops should go to real code-run (gap 9). A rewritten-state format is the right shape for long traces.

source: Abdollahi et al. (2025) Demystifying Errors in LLM Reasoning Traces: An Empirical Study of Code Execution Simulation (error taxonomy)
finding: Reasoning models predict output well (85-98%). Their trace errors fall into nine types: computation, indexing, control flow, skipped statements, misreported final output, input misread, native-API misevaluation, hallucination, lack of verification. None of the nine is aliasing, reference or mutation.
numbers: 427 snippets from HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench; DeepSeek-R1, GPT-o4-mini, Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash. Computation errors dominate: e.g. HumanEval+ regular inputs 16/20/7/10 per model (Claude/DeepSeek/Gemini/GPT), edge inputs 27/28/34/47; LiveCodeBench edge inputs 101/114/59/69. Control flow errors far fewer (e.g. Claude 13 on LiveCodeBench regular).
limits: Benchmarks are mostly algorithmic functions with immutable or fresh data, so they rarely stress aliasing. Absence of the category is weak evidence, not a measurement of alias errors. Only reasoning-class models.
agent_relevance: For frontier reasoning models, value computation, not reference semantics, is the main trace error. Gap 6 is not closed: nobody has measured alias errors directly. Edge inputs cause more errors than regular ones (gap 8).

source: Abdollahi et al. (2025) Demystifying Errors in LLM Reasoning Traces: An Empirical Study of Code Execution Simulation (tool fix)
finding: Replacing the faulty arithmetic step with a real computed result, and asking the model to continue, fixed most computation errors.
numbers: Computation errors before/after tool support: Gemini 2.5 82 to 36; GPT-4o mini 71 to 32; Claude 4 Sonnet 131 to 56; DeepSeek R1 155 to 57. Total 439 to 181, 58.8% fixed (paper says 58%). About 40% remained.
limits: Authors wrote the correct clause by hand, so this is an upper bound for an automatic tool step. Only the computation category tested.
agent_relevance: Real computation spliced into the trace is cheap and effective, supporting a hybrid S2: model plans steps, interpreter computes values. Gap 9.

source: Spiess, Devanbu, Barr (2026) How Robustly do LLMs Understand Execution Semantics? (cross-opened)
finding: On the original CRUXEval GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro score about 99%. After meaning-preserving code changes and variable renaming GPT-5.2 falls a lot; Gemini 3 Pro hardly moves. Open reasoning models are lower but stable.
numbers: GPT-5.2 99.24% canonical, about 76.4% under renaming/transformations (McNemar p<.001); Gemini 3 Pro 99.24% to 95.79% and 98.37%. GPT-5.2 input perturbation: roughly 79.6 to 56.1 (-19.5) in one table. DeepSeek-R1 family 38 to 67% and stable. Models often not consistent (all right or all wrong) even on a dense neighbourhood of one input.
limits: Preprint v1. Tables in the text extraction were partly garbled; headline numbers cross-checked with abstract (20-24 points decline). Vendors' model names as reported by the authors. Perturbation measures robustness of a single-pass answer, not of a scaffolded trace.
agent_relevance: A correct answer on one input does not show understanding. A mutated-input re-run (gap 8) is a cheap way to test a trace; this paper tests only plain prompting, so the scaffold version is still untested.

source: Spiess, Devanbu, Barr (2026) How Robustly do LLMs Understand Execution Semantics? (prompt sensitivity on exceptions)
finding: Adding one sentence about the language behaviour to the prompt (tell the model to predict exceptions, with the type and message) changed accuracy more than model choice. This is a tiny written rule sheet.
numbers: GPT-5.2 on exception-raising inputs improved from 15.00% to 81.00% when prompted to track exceptions (authors' threats section). Combined prompt (type-strict + exceptions + one example) raised original, perturbed and PSR scores for GPT-5 Nano and Gemini 3 Pro, but GPT-5.2 fell 81% to 76% on non-exception cases: about 4% of its previously right answers became wrongly predicted exceptions.
quote: Performance was highly dependent on instruction; for example, GPT-5.2 improved from 15.00% to 81.00% when prompted to track exceptions.
limits: Not a general semantic rule sheet; one rule (exceptions exist). Over-correction shown: the rule over-triggered. Single run, no repeats stated.
agent_relevance: Nearest evidence to gap 1: a written semantic rule can lift accuracy a lot on the cases it covers, but can cause false triggers elsewhere. A rule sheet needs a check on ordinary cases too.

source: Carleton University thesis (2022) Investigating the Utility of Notional Machine Instruction in an Introductory Programming Lesson
finding: Independent test of the notional-machine idea in a tutor. Two tutor versions, one with an explicit notional machine and one without. Both groups learned; no difference between them.
numbers: N = 48 novices. Learning = pretest-to-posttest gain adjusted for prior knowledge. Abstract: learning increased overall but no significant difference between groups. No statistics given in the abstract.
quote: Learning increased overall, but there was no significant difference in learning between groups.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the thesis text. Master's thesis, not peer reviewed. N = 48, so low power; it is not a formal replication of PLTutor and the tutor differs. Short lesson.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to K05: teaching an explicit machine did not add learning beyond video lessons plus self-explanation. Gap 7: no N > 100 study found. The one independent test we found is a null at N = 48.

source: Savelka et al. (2023) Large Language Models (GPT) Struggle to Answer Multiple-Choice Questions about Code
finding: Old GPT models did worse on multiple-choice questions with code than without, and worst on questions that ask what the code does or what is true of it.
numbers: 530 MCQs from three Python courses. text-davinci-003 and similar: 59.5% on code-snippet MCQs vs 77.9% on no-code ones (overall 65.5% best model). Completion-style MCQs 87.1% vs 60.1% for others. Output-prediction and true/false items hardest (e.g. true/false 18-27% for the weakest model).
limits: 2023 models, no CoT, MCQ format (guessing helps). Does not separate reference/aliasing from value questions; so gap 6 is not answered.
agent_relevance: Historical baseline for the weak-model side of the trace gate. Shows that analysis questions, not syntax, were hard for LLMs, as for novices.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (boundary: who gains from revision)
finding: Revision pays off only for the stronger model on the harder set, and mostly at larger budgets. For weaker models, spending the same tokens on fresh samples is as good or better.
numbers: APPS: only GPT-4 benefits significantly from self-repair (nf=nr=1); Code Llama and GPT-3.5 match or lag the no-repair baseline. HumanEval: Code Llama and GPT-3.5 show gains, GPT-4 omitted (near ceiling). At small budgets gains are marginal or non-existent.
limits: Different from trace-vs-direct crossover but same shape: the extra reasoning step helps only above a model-strength threshold that depends on the task. No cheap per-task detector was tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: no study gives a clean per-task crossover detector; a small pilot with equal-token resampling as the control is the only tested design.
